description:
TourbillionSG is a team from Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam: two AI engineers, two data analysts and two full-stack developers. Our name stands for S (space), G (gravity) and SG (Saigon). A tourbillon is a watch mechanism built to cancel the effect of gravity, and we want to study what fire does when gravity is gone.

Why join us: we have a clear plan, defined roles for each person, and a strict rule that every number must come from a cited source.
summary: FlameGuard AI is a web dashboard that turns NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) combustion archive into traceable fire-safety insights for crewed spacecraft, lunar bases, Mars habitats and pressurized rovers. It catalogs 24 NASA PSI investigations and 1,926 source records. Its research assistant searches 2,508 passages from CC0-licensed PSI sources and 66 passages from NASA-authored articles, answers questions in English or Vietnamese by quoting those passages verbatim with citations, and declines requests for safe/unsafe verdicts. Users can browse and compare investigations across the three fire-safety pillars (prevention, detection and suppression); inspect fuels, sample geometry, oxygen, pressure and flow conditions; and enter a mission scenario, such as an illustrative lunar-habitat scenario at 30% O₂ and 10.2 psia, to find related studies and, just as importantly, see where evidence is missing, including partial gravity, which is not represented in our imported collection.
details:
What it does

FlameGuard AI is an evidence-first dashboard for NASA microgravity combustion research. It has five parts:

• Research Dashboard: an overview of the indexed PSI investigations, their source coverage and the partial-gravity evidence gap.

• Experiment Explorer: lets you filter investigations by fire-safety pillar (prevention, detection, suppression), fuel type and platform. Opening a study shows its objectives and, where available, sample geometry, sensors, test records with original values and units, and the exact source file behind each value. Studies can be compared side by side.

• Mission Scenario & Gap Matrix: you describe a habitat scenario by oxygen, pressure, gravity, airflow, material and purpose. The backend ranks related investigations and shows, test record by test record, which related conditions match, differ or are unknown. Missing evidence, such as lunar or Martian gravity, is shown as a gap rather than filled in.

• Research assistant: a retrieval-based assistant (BM25 extractive retrieval with English and Vietnamese query support) that answers only by quoting admitted NASA passages. Each quote cites its source file, locator and hash. It declines to answer safety-verdict questions, off-topic questions, and questions about partial-gravity data that does not exist.

• Flame Studio and Resources: interactive 3D flame visualizations, plus the challenge's official NASA resources. The 3D scenes are qualitative illustrations informed by cited experiment reports.

How we built the data

The data release was built from official NASA PSI files and metadata. Selected NASA articles provide additional context, and separate experiment reports inform Flame Studio.

• 24 combustion investigations, 1,926 source records and 2,574 passages. The investigations include FLEX, BASS/BASS-II, Saffire-I/II/III, SAME/SAME-R, ACME BRE/CFI-G/E-FIELD/s-Flame, CFI, SPICE, SLICE and DAFT.

• The 2,574 citable passages are 2,508 from CC0-licensed PSI sources plus 66 from six NASA-authored articles.

• PSI-10 (Flame Design) is listed as a catalog reference only. Its reuse rights are not confirmed, so it contributes no records or passages.

• Sources include PSI experimental tables, science documents, raw data samples, the ACME Chamber Calculator workbooks and the CFI Data Summary Spreadsheet.

• We kept original units, null values and conflicting values. For example, the two different initial droplet diameters reported for FLEX-007 are both kept.

• We did not invent test runs from day-summary tables, and we did not treat burner oxygen or apparatus flow as cabin conditions. Calculator values are labelled as derived.

• Every record traces back to the original bytes through a SHA-256 hash and a source-specific locator, such as a CSV row, spreadsheet cell, JSON field, or article paragraph.

Benefits and impact

Researchers, students and engineers can find relevant microgravity fire-safety evidence quickly, compare reported conditions and measurements while preserving differences in units and experimental setup, and see exactly what has and has not been tested. This matters as NASA plans higher-oxygen, lower-pressure atmospheres for lunar bases and pressurized rovers. Making evidence gaps visible also helps prioritize future experiments, such as partial-gravity combustion.

Tools and technologies

• Frontend: Next.js 15, React 19, TypeScript, TanStack Query, Framer Motion and Three.js.

• Backend: Python, FastAPI, SQLAlchemy, Alembic and PostgreSQL.

• Retrieval: BM25 extractive retrieval with citation checks. The research assistant uses extractive retrieval and citation checks. It does not call a generative model at runtime.

• Deployment: Docker on Azure Container Apps.

• Source code: https://github.com/hieuduong1810/TourbillionSG-FlameInFreefall

What makes it different

Our main design principle is honesty about evidence:

• Relevance scores are not risk probabilities, and the research assistant declines requests for safe/unsafe verdicts.

• Microgravity results are never presented as lunar or Martian data.

• Source-record counts are not presented as counts of independent experiments.

• No record is labelled as scientifically reviewed.

Use of SI tools

The team used SI coding assistants (Claude Code and OpenAI Codex) for coding, debugging, research, data analysis and documentation writing. The team reviewed and tested all SI-assisted code and data processing. The deployed product does not use generative AI to produce answers.

• Claude Code: data pipeline code (PSI acquisition, workbook parsing and the release builder), tests, documentation, and drafting this submission text.

• OpenAI Codex: coding and debugging, and reviewing the visualizations, data sources and licences against the original NASA documents.

• Checks on SI-assisted work: automated tests for the data release, export and retrieval, backend tests on a test PostgreSQL database, linting, a test that every spreadsheet locator points to its original cell, and spot checks of values against PSI source files such as FLEX-007.
